svg.font-family: Inter, Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
svg.title: Figure 1. Two different machines, one name
svg.desc: A comparison of two things both called a self-hosted VPN. The first is a tunnel endpoint on hardware you already own at home, which gives you a residential address, reaches the devices on your home network, and costs nothing each month, but cannot change your apparent country and hides nothing from your own internet provider. The second is a tunnel endpoint on a rented server in a datacentre, which gives you an exit address in a country you choose and a genuinely static address, but costs fifty to seventy-five dollars a year, cannot reach anything at home, and places the hosting company in your trust path. A table below maps the five usual use cases to the machine that actually serves each one, showing that two of the five are served only by the machine at home, which this lesson does not build.
svg.text: Figure 1: Two Different Machines, Both Called "Self-Hosted"
The usual case lists reaching your home network first. The usual build then rents a server that cannot reach it.
A. ON HARDWARE YOU ALREADY OWN
a router, a spare small computer, a device already running at home

g.text: What it gives you
A residential address, which almost nothing blocks.
Reachable devices at home: files, printers, cameras, services.
No monthly bill and no account rented in your name.
What it costs
Nothing each month. One port opened at the router, a name that
follows a changing address, and hardware that stays powered on.
What it cannot do
Change the country you appear to be in.
Hide anything from your own internet provider, who is the one
network that still sees both ends of everything you do.
Help at all if your home upload speed is the constraint.
The usual case names this first. The usual build never provides it.

svg.text: B. ON HARDWARE SOMEBODY ELSE OWNS
a rented virtual server in a datacentre, which is what this lesson builds

g.text: What it gives you
An exit address in a country you pick from a list.
A genuinely fixed address, which is the strongest reason to do this.
Upload speed far better than most home connections.
What it costs
Roughly 50 to 75 US dollars a year, plus traffic above the
included allowance. About four hours to build and half an hour
a month to keep. And the hosting company joins your trust path.
What it cannot do
Reach one single device on your home network.
Give you anonymity. It reduces it, and Figure 2 sets out why.
Escape the datacentre address blocks many services apply.
This is a hosting exercise. It is a good one, for the right reasons.

svg.text: Two of the five are served only, or better, by a machine at home. The rented-server build never considers that option.
Before you rent anything, decide which of these two machines your actual reason requires. They are not the same product.
